title: Photograph birds without hurting them

scenes.headline: Get the shot without harming the bird
If it flies off or changes behaviour, you're too close
scenes.body: Use a longer lens and let the bird carry on as normal.

scenes.headline: Keep your distance from nests
scenes.body: Keep visits brief: people nearby can keep parents away from eggs and chicks.

scenes.headline: No bait. No call playback.
scenes.body: Recorded calls can pull a parent off its nest. Wait for natural moments like this kingfisher's own catch.

scenes.headline: Think before you share a location
scenes.body: A pinned nest or roost can draw crowds. Weigh the impact on the bird first.

caption:
The best bird photo is one the bird never noticed.

Audubon also advises using flash sparingly, if at all, and avoiding it entirely on owls and other night birds.

Source: National Audubon Society, Guide to Ethical Bird Photography.  Photos/video: Wikimedia Commons (credits on screen).
notes: Ethics how-to mixing full shots and cards; four rules from Audubon's guide, illustrated with Indian species (peafowl in Corbett, grey hornbills in Sangli) and a wild hornbill clip.
